script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. In this session of our sustainable architecture series, I want to talk about a technology that is very old but is attracting a great deal of new interest: the windcatcher. A windcatcher is a tall tower on top of a building, designed to bring cooler air down into the rooms below without any machinery.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Windcatchers are most closely associated with Iran and the countries around the Persian Gulf, although similar structures appear in Egypt and Pakistan. Exactly how old they are is debated. Some of the surviving towers are only a few hundred years old, but ancient Egyptian paintings show something very similar, which suggests the idea goes back more than three thousand years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So how do they work? There are really two mechanisms. The first is simple. The openings at the top of the tower face the direction of the prevailing wind, that is, the wind that blows most often in that location. Air enters the tower, is forced downwards, and flows through the house.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The second mechanism works even when there's no wind at all. During the day, the tower is heated by the sun. Warm air inside the building rises up the tower and escapes at the top, and this draws in cooler air from lower openings, often from a shaded courtyard. Engineers call this the stack effect, and it's the same principle that makes a chimney work.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: In the city of Yazd, in central Iran, builders went a step further. In some houses, before entering the rooms, the air was led over an underground water channel called a qanat. The water cooled the air further, and the result was something surprisingly close to modern air conditioning. Some of these houses even had cool rooms for storing food in summer.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Why are architects interested in windcatchers today? Mostly because conventional air conditioning uses huge amounts of electricity, and in hot countries it can account for over half of a building's energy use. A windcatcher, by contrast, needs no electricity at all. And it has no moving parts to break down.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: That's not to say they're perfect. There are some real drawbacks. They're less effective in humid climates, where cooling the air doesn't make people feel much more comfortable. And because they're open at the top, dust and insects can get into the building. Traditional builders sometimes hung damp cloths in the tower to catch the dust, but insects remain a problem, especially in summer.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Now, let's look at how modern designers have adapted the idea, with three recent examples. I'll go through them quite quickly, so you may want to take notes.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The first is a primary school. Many people assume that projects like this are all in the Middle East, but this one is in Portugal, in the south of the country, where summers are now regularly above forty degrees.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The school has twin towers, and the clever part is that they're fitted with automatic louvres, small angled panels that open and close depending on the temperature and wind speed. Teachers report that classrooms are now about four degrees cooler on the hottest days.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The second example is a shopping centre in England. Here the designers used rotating cowls on top of the towers. These turn like weather vanes so that the opening always faces into the wind. The centre's managers originally predicted they would save around twenty per cent of the energy used for cooling, but the actual figure turned out to be higher, at thirty per cent.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The final example is a housing estate in Australia, next to a very busy main road. Residents there were worried that windcatchers would let in traffic fumes, but the air quality inside has actually been fine. What surprised the architects was a different benefit. Because the towers are fitted with an acoustic lining, the homes don't need windows facing the road to be opened, and residents report far less noise from the street.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So, I hope that gives you a sense of how an ancient technology is being reinvented. Next week, we'll look at the computer modelling that engineers use to design these towers.
